page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.g5.8xlarge is a general-purpose instance powered by an Intel Xeon 8163 processor operating at a base frequency of 2.5 GHz. Built on the x86_64 architecture using KVM virtualization, it offers 16 physical cores provisioned as 32 dedicated vCPUs with two threads per core. Memory capacity stands at 128 GB, yielding a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU. The CPU configuration features a 35 MB L3 cache alongside support for instruction extensions such as AVX-512 and AES encryption. This instance features no bundled local storage and includes a baseline network throughput of 10 Gbps without dedicated GPUs.

In performance testing, the instance exhibits middle-tier multi-core capability balanced against lower per-core performance. Single-core benchmarks place in the bottom 25%, with single-threaded gzip compression dropping into the lower 10%. Conversely, multi-threaded workloads utilize the full 32-vCPU capacity effectively, achieving average benchmark scores in multi-core stress-ng, Passmark, software compilation via Clang, and bzip3 decompression. Memory bandwidth testing shows consistent average performance across both cached and large uncached read/write operations. Small and medium LLM inference tasks, as well as Redis SET operations and static web serving, demonstrate solid middle-range throughput.

The ecs.g5.8xlarge instance provides cost-effective scaling for distributed application components that rely on multi-threaded execution rather than single-threaded CPU speed. Given its balanced 1:4 memory allocation and lack of integrated local SSD storage, persistent data requirements rely on external cloud storage attachment. The instance fits general enterprise workloads, middle-tier web servers, caching layers like Redis, application servers, and moderate container orchestration nodes where multi-core parallelization compensates for modest single-threaded speed.

This hardware profile provides a cost-effective platform for multi-threaded workloads, enterprise application tiers, web serving, in-memory caching, and software build pipelines where parallel execution offsets individual core speed constraints.
